This alludes to the great controversy sparked by the Mu’tazilite doctrine that the Qur’an is not eternal but created. In AD 833, Caliph Ma’mûn imposed this doctrine as an article of faith. A period of fanatical inquisition followed, during which the “orthodox”—including the “old believer” Ibn Hanbal—suffered persecution. About fifteen years later, Caliph Motawakkil, Ma’mûn’s third successor, reversed the situation in favour of the orthodox theologians for reasons of high politics. The arguments for and against the Qur’an’s eternity have sometimes been compared to arguments about Christ’s two natures in the Christological controversies. Yet even if one invokes al-Ash’arî’s reconciliation (the Qur’an as eternal Word, its letters and ink as human productions), we must not forget that the question raised by the esoteric interpretation of Sufism and Shiism is not of the same kind as the questions addressed by the orthodox Christology of the Councils. The relation of zâhir to bâtin—outward to hidden, earthly to heavenly, Nâtiq to Sâmit (Speaking Prophet to Silent Imam), literal meaning to prophetic spiritual meaning—reflects an entirely different conception and concern. Its distinctive expression is ultimately found in the doctrine of the Imams, in the language of theophany, and it follows the pattern of a Christology other than the orthodox one: in broad outline, rather the Christology of the Ebionites or the Melchizedekians, with the pre-eminent significance of Christ’s baptism, its interpretation through the idea of Christos Angelos, and so on. See also below, p. 302, note 117, and our edition of Mollâ Sadrâ Shîrâzî, Le Livre des pénétrations métaphysiques, index under “Word” and “Book.” ↩

Sadr Torkeh Ispahânî, a brother or cousin of the preceding figure, executed on Shâhrokh’s orders in 850 AH. (4) Afzaloddin Moh. Torkeh, military judge (Qâdî ’askar) under the Safavid ruler Shâh Tahmâsp (930–984 AH / 1524–1576). ↩
Golshan-e Râz, “The Rose Garden of Mystery.” On Shams Lâhijî’s commentary on this poem and the Ismaili glosses, see Part III of our Trilogie ismaélienne. ↩

Risâla-ye shaqq-e qamar. We quote this short work from a Persian miscellany (majmû’a), Département d’Iran manuscript 29, copied in 1294 AH (250 × 165 mm, 21 lines per page), containing: (1) the Mi’râj-Nâmah attributed to Avicenna (long version, including the opening moqaddama), pp. 1–27; (2) Shaqq-e Qamar, pp. 28–39; and (3) biographies of three Shia figures (Shaykh Mofîd, Mortazâ ’Alam al-Hodâ, Mîr Dâmâd), pp. 40–57. ↩

Ke be ’Aql-e fa’âl paywandad wayâd ba â yakî shawad. Sa’inoddin alludes to two opposing interpretations: conjunction with the Active Intelligence while preserving individuality; or unification, in which the soul’s being merges and becomes indistinguishable from the Active Intelligence. Avicenna and Suhrawardî vigorously defended the first conception. ↩

In fact, the structure of this angelology varies. The perfect set of ten Intelligences is not exclusively Avicennian; it also has a firm foundation in the Ismaili Hamîdoddîn Kermânî’s principle of the “balance” (mizân) or “symbolism of the worlds” (tawâzon al-’awâlim). In some schemes, the First Intelligence, as Primum Movens (First Mover), is raised above the whole Pleroma; in others, the Active Intelligence is identified with the Intelligence of the Heaven of the Moon or treated as a distinct Intelligence proceeding from it. Thus, depending on the case, we may have nine, ten, or eleven Intelligences (Angeli intellectuales). See our Avicenne et le Récit visionnaire, vol. I, p. 117, and vol. II, pp. 107–108. ↩
In Persian: Ân-tche î bâd o hast o khwâhad bâd, jomla dar khweshtan be-yâb ke hast. ↩

Note the corresponding terms: Arabic sohûr (epiphanic state), Persian paydâ’î, howayda shudan; Arabic izhâr (the act or function of revealing, of making something appear), Persian paydâkunandagî, howayda gardânîdan. ↩
On these “descents” (tanazzolât) and the hierarchy of planes of being, or “Presences” or “Dignities” (Hazârât), see our Soufisme d’Ibn ’Arabî, pp. 262–263, notes 233–234. ↩

Sâ’inoddîn calls them arbâb-e ’ilm-e horûf-e qorânî: those who read the mysterious letters placed at the beginning of certain Qur’anic suras as symbols or ideograms, “abbreviations for classes of concepts spelled out to the Prophet in a dream” (L. Massignon). See our Avicenne ..., pp. 320 ff. ↩

On the foundations of this method, see Gershom Scholem, Die Bedeutung der Thora in der jüdischen Mystik (Diogenes 14/15, 1957), and, for detailed applications, C. D. Ginsburg, The Kabbalah, reprinted 1956, pp. 131 ff. We should not forget that the earliest systematic attempts to explore the symbolic values of the alphabet’s letters appear in the Greek Gnosis of Asia. As early as the eighth century, the Shia Gnostic Moghîra (d. 737 at Kufa) spoke of “the twenty-eight Arabic letters that came from the fall of God’s Supreme Name upon his Crown” (see our Avicenne ..., vol. I, p. 321). On Hurufi interpretation, see Clément Huart, Textes persans relatifs à la secte des Houroufis (Gibb Memorial Series IX), London, 1909, pp. 284 ff., concerning abjad-e hisâbî (gematria, the practice of assigning numerical values to the letters of a word and explaining the word by comparison with another of equal value). There is a simple or abbreviated calculation (hisâb jomlî): treat each letter of a word as an arithmetic unit and add the values. There is also an analytic calculation (hisâb tafsîlî): break each word down into letters, write out the sound-name of each letter, count every resulting letter as one unit, remove repetitions, and add them together. The Gnostic Marcus already proceeded in exactly this way. We cannot trace in detail here the correspondence between the rules used by Kabbalistic interpretation and those of the Ismailis and Hurufis, but a study of them would be well worth undertaking. ↩

See Huart, op. cit., pp. 219 ff. While Huart’s edition of the texts remains extremely valuable, serious reservations must be made about the “Étude sur la religion des Houroufis par le Dr Riza Tevfiq,” included in the French part of the book. The mocking tone frequently adopted by the author is all the more painful because his ridicule falls not on the doctrines themselves but on the banality to which his own fundamental misunderstanding reduces them. See Hellmut Ritter’s substantial recent study, Die Anfänge der Hurûfisekte (Oriens 7/1, 1954). ↩
See the passage from the Haqîqat-Nâmeh quoted in Huart, ibid., p. 242. Riza Tevfiq’s translation should, of course, be revised. ↩

On the “maternal inscriptions” or lines of the face, see Huart, ibid., p. 289. On the Prophet’s hadith (“On the night of the Mi’râj, I saw my Lord in the form of a handsome, beardless youth”), see our Soufisme d’Ibn ’Arabî, pp. 203 ff. (the hadith of the vision). ↩
On the Hurufi interpretation of Abraham, Moses, and Muhammad, see ibid., pp. 263–268; compare Rûzbehân’s interpretation in his Yasmîn. ↩

On the fundamental Ismaili Shia distinction between the Enunciator, the Speaker or Prophet (Nâtiq), and the Silent One or Imam (Sâmit), see our two studies, Le Livre du Glorieux de Jâbir ibn Hayyân (Eranos-Jahrbuch XVIII, 1950), pp. 67 ff., and Gnose ismaélienne (ibid., XXIII, 1955), pp. 195 ff.; also our Trilogie ismaélienne, index under Nâtiq. Note also that in the great vision forming the prologue to Ibn ’Arabî’s Fotûhât, the Youth appearing to him is called Nâtiq-Sâmit, the Speaking-Silent One (see our Soufisme d’Ibn ’Arabî, p. 208). Here the Imam, as the Silent One, is mentally identified with perfect human beauty. The Imam is the hidden meaning of Beauty as the “speaking Qur’an,” or as the Imam who “speaks” through his very silence. ↩

Recall that in Ismaili imamology, the Imam is the earthly representative and pole of the Tenth Intelligence, the spiritual Adam (Adam rûhânî) or Angel-Anthropos, corresponding to Gabriel as Holy Spirit and Active Intelligence among the Ishrâqiyûn. See our Trilogie ismaélienne, index under Tenth Intelligence. ↩

That is why this recapitulation presupposes the Shia conception. According to Sâ’inoddîn, all spiritual people have recognized in a general way that the fullness of spiritual meaning emanates from this Perfect Form (the Imam as heavenly Anthropos). But they have been unable to analyse it in detail or understand all its circumstances, even though they possessed knowledge of the Return and its destination. For example, they could not really grasp the allusions of eschatology: the settling of accounts, the Balance, the appearance and representative forms of human deeds. An Ismaili theosopher would speak in just this way of philosophers whom he respects, but who lacked the key of ta’wîl needed to understand what eschatological images ultimately refer to, including the splitting of the Moon mentioned in our verse. ↩

The text also makes a veiled allusion here to the Yajfr, a mysterious book originating in the Tablets of Moses, passed down from Imam to Imam since ’Alî ibn Abî-Tâlib, and revealing the secrets of events in every past and future age. See Saffîna I, p. 165. ↩

Dabestân-e Madhâhib, Bombay, 1267, pp. 263–264. The transition is straightforward. The author states that up to this point he has been reporting Avicenna’s views; now he will relate what he has learned from another book by the theosophical sages. A long exposition follows, in which we recognize several passages literally agreeing with Sâ’inoddîn’s text but supplemented by the details on which we shall now focus. (We have already noted that Shea and Troyer’s old and inadequate English translation of the Dabestân is completely unusable; Book II, note 500.) ↩
See our Trilogie ismaélienne, p. 162, note 43. ↩

The idea attributed here to Suhrawardî’s Ishrâqiyûn is typically Ismaili. The Cycle of Prophecy begins with the First Intelligence of the Pleroma (or Archangel Logos), which summons the other Intelligences emanating from it to tawhîd, the affirmation of divine unity. By undertaking this summons (da’wat), it becomes the first Nabî, or prophet. Although it is called the spiritual Adam (Adam ma’nawî) here, we must remember that in Ismailism the designation Adam rûhânî (the “pneumatic” or spiritual Adam) is reserved for the Third Intelligence. It was the protagonist of the drama that brought it down from the third rank to the tenth, where it is henceforth functionally identified with the Archangel Gabriel as the Active Intelligence of Illuminationist Avicennism. Yet the pair formed by the First and Second Intelligences, from which the Third proceeded, is also called the Adam-and-Eve of the Pleroma. This explains the designation found in the Dabestân. We still need to analyse further, within Ismailism, the intimate relation between the Angel-Anthropos and the Angel-Logos from which it proceeds, the latter being invested with the divine Name above all names (Al-Lâh). Ismaili metaphysics has perceived the drama of humanity as a drama within the divine world. See our Trilogie ismaélienne, index under Intelligence. ↩

Agar sad hazâr rasûl mathalan khwâd-râ ’ayn-e ’Aql-e fa’âl girand, khâtam al-rosol and. The author ends his account with a couplet by Gharîzî: “From my feet to my head, my being has become the Beloved. If henceforth I wish to see myself, my Beloved stands before me as my mirror.” This implies a connection of ideas resembling that established by the Fedeli d’amore between the Active Intelligence and Madonna Intelligenza. As for the idea of parwarda (a being nurtured or reared), compare Avicenna’s gloss in the margin of the so-called Theology of Aristotle, which speaks of the care with which the angelic Intelligences adorn and perfect the soul, treating it as their child. See our Avicenne ..., p. 88. ↩
